items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.

items.summary: In this work, we study a fractional diffusion model in time and space, formulated in an open and bounded domain, involving a Caputo fractional derivative of order $μ\in(0,1)$ with respect to a time scale function $Ψ$, together with a spectral fractional Laplacian operator of order $s\in(0,1)$. The associated direct problem is analyzed, as well as the inverse problem of temporal reconstruction from final data, which is inherently ill-posed. Through a spectral representation, the instability of the problem and the effect of the choice of the function $Ψ$ on the amplification of spectral modes are examined.
items.title: Backward Homogeneous Heat Equation with $Ψ$-Caputo Time Derivative and Spectral Fractional Laplacian

items.summary: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.
items.title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models

items.summary: This paper demonstrates an objective method of computing monthly mean 700-mb height anomalies (H) at 108 grid points in the Western Hemisphere for a 40-yr period as a function of concurrent anomalies of monthly mean sea level pressure (P), at the same 108 points used for H, and monthly mean surface air temperature (T) averaged over 112 areas in North America. The authors applied a forward stepwise program to derive linear multiple regression equations that explained 81% of the variance of H by means of only 3.5 variables, averaged over all months and grid points. The stability of these equations held up well on 6 yr of independent data in terms of explained variance, root-mean-square error, and the spatial anomaly correlation coefficient. Therefore, it seems feasible to reconstruct maps of H for the first half of the twentieth century as a function of data on P and T only. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.
items.title: Reconstruction of Monthly Mean 700-mb Heights from Surface Data by Reverse Specification - FGDC XML metadata artifact

items.summary: Precomputed demo datasets for Luxar , a system for compiling and visualising arbitrary-sized nD scientific scenes in the browser. These files are expensive to compute (GPU fitting, in some cases hours) and are hosted here so the software repository stays small and installable. Every file is a derived product: a Gaussian-splat fit, a decimated level-of-detail structure, or an extracted point catalog. None of them is the raw source imagery. The upstream sources are cited per dataset below, and users of this record should cite the upstream source in addition to this record. Licensing This record groups datasets whose upstream licences permit redistribution with attribution: CC BY 4.0, CC0 1.0, and United States federal public domain. The record carries a single CC BY 4.0 stamp because Zenodo permits one licence per record, and CC BY is the most restrictive of that set; the effective licence of an individual file is the one listed against it below. Datasets under ShareAlike terms are kept in a separate record, because ShareAlike survives derivation and would otherwise contaminate this one. How the Gaussian-splat files were produced Each source volume was fitted with the Luxar gsplat pipeline ( luxar gsplat fit ) on a GPU. These are lossy representations built for visualisation and interactive exploration; they are not a substitute for the source imagery in quantitative analysis. Choosing the splat count. The number of Gaussians K was calibrated per dataset by Noise2Self blind-spot cross-validation ( luxar gsplat cal ), and then checked by refitting at the candidate count and scoring the reconstruction against the whole source volume. The second step is not a formality. items.summary: Generative-prior-based super-resolution (SR) methods leverage implicit knowledge learned from large-scale models to enhance low-resolution inputs. However, such priors are inherently stochastic and optimized for diverse generation, conflicting with the deterministic, high-fidelity reconstruction required for SR. It is also tied to the base model, costly to update, and prone to hallucinations as real-world data evolves. To address these limitations, we introduce WorldSR, a novel framework that augments SR with explicit, entity-aligned visual world knowledge. WorldSR automatically decomposes the input into semantic entities and performs entity-wise retrieval of structurally and semantically aligned images from a large-scale external corpus. For efficiency and reliability, we incorporate a memory mechanism to reuse previously retrieved results and a multi-step filtering process to refine candidate references. The selected references as world knowledge are then integrated through a novel multi-reference super-resolution model, which provides fine-grained constraints for detail synthesis and structural recovery. Experiments on real-world SR benchmarks show that WorldSR consistently improves structural fidelity and visual quality, outperforming existing generative super-resolution methods. Our results suggest that entity-level grounding in external visual world knowledge provides a simple and effective complement to model-bound generative priors.
items.title: WorldSR: Harnessing World Knowledge Search for Grounded Image Super-Resolution

items.summary: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
items.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
items.title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

items.summary: This dataset provides supporting numerical artifacts for the manuscript “Reduced-Regularity Consistency for a Direct ABC-Adapted L1-Type Operator: Analysis and Diffusion Benchmarks.” The archive contains the locked Problem-1 FDM/FEM common-resolution results, the Chebyshev spectral results, the Problem-1 temporal-contamination audit and its derived summary, the Problem-2 Q=64 FDM/Spectral graded-mesh validation results, and the FEM Pilot-2 console-verified summary. A README, artifact manifest, and SHA-256 checksum list document the archive contents, integrity checks, evidence status, and item-specific limitations. This is a supporting-data archive, not a complete source-code or computational-environment release. The archived CSV files were retained from the project artifacts and integrity-checked during packaging; the original numerical experiments were not rerun for this deposit. The FEM Pilot-2 file is a console-verified summary rather than a complete raw export. Known provenance limitations are documented in the accompanying README and manifest. The Q=64 results show refinement trends consistent with the stated consistency upper bound for the tested cases. They do not establish sharpness of the estimate or an unconditional fully discrete convergence theorem.

Starting material, cell genealogy, material flow, agent action, calibration, environmental state, contamination evidence, identity, purity, maturation, and blind terminal function remain linked throughout production. Personalization changes the process path but never waives the release contract. Thirty physicalized models connect stochastic lot release, population dynamics, clonal diversity, living-product mass balance, contamination transport, Bayesian sterility, microfluidic residence time, oxygen and thermal transport, scaffold maturation, viscoelasticity, adhesion injury, swarm allocation, fault-bounded consensus, common-cause reliability, calibration drift, sensor fusion, change detection, small-lot inference, potency, multivariate release, logistics, recipe portability, provenance, economics, and robust joint qualification. Eighty-two chapters each open with a governing gold equation and develop five one-page research sections. Two hundred Research Gates challenge the system with donor shift, contamination, agent failure, supply interruption, calibration drift, reagent substitution, incomplete genealogy, and blinded transfer to a second laboratory. Contamination, identity failure, unclosed genealogy, invalid calibration, and failed independent function are noncompensable vetoes. items.summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. items.summary: This is a study commissioned by the Panel for the Future of Science and Technology, European Parliament: Generative Artificial Intelligence could strengthen open science by improving accessibility, findability, and usability. Still, under less favourable conditions, it could also weaken scientific exchange by obscuring provenance, deepening dependency on opaque infrastructures, and reinforcing inequalities and increasing synthetic overload, in which large volumes of AI-generated scientific content overwhelm the capacity of researchers and systems to verify, interpret, and trust information. This study describes how Generative AI is reshaping scientific exchange within the broader framework of open science. It shows that the main policy challenge is not whether Generative AI will be used in scientific exchange, but under what institutional, infrastructural, and normative conditions it can support reliable research, and knowledge valorisation. The European Union should treat scientific exchange as public-interest infrastructure and enact policies to support skills, strengthened provenance, transparency, reproducibility, inclusion, and strategic capacity in an AI-mediated research environment. This report provides specific policy options tackling the risks that can be associated with the use of AI in scientific exchange. This study is prepared for, and addressed to, the Members and staff of the European Parliament as background material to assist them in their parliamentary work. The content of the document is the sole responsibility of its author(s) and any opinions expressed herein should not be taken to represent an official position of the Parliament.

items.summary: Multi-agent systems rely on communication to complete tasks, and latent communication passes continuous representations to reduce text generation and re-encoding. However, multi-agent systems must reconfigure agent models, whereas existing latent-communication methods are built for fixed model combinations, so their interfaces may fail after replacement. Our pilot study confirms this interface failure and identifies the requirement for interface reuse after model replacement. We present LatBridge, which connects agent models through a shared Bridge and separate interfaces under a shared latent-communication protocol. After agent model replacement, LatBridge reuses unchanged interfaces, selects matching low-rank interfaces, and combines them through the Bridge, training only missing ones with all models frozen. The Bridge processes source representations in the basic mode and constructs target input without autoregressive generation in the accelerated mode. Experiments support effective communication after model replacement, with mean basic-mode accuracies of 14.8% on MATH and 27.3% on ALFWorld next-action prediction across eight small-model configurations. Analyses examine the factors supporting task accuracy and communication efficiency.
items.title: LatBridge: Efficient and Stable Model Replacement in Latent-Communication Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.
items.title: Reproducibility Package for Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift

items.summary: A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations. We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these predictions using a sampled energy objective. Our model learns distinct continuations on constructed multimodal tasks and captures latent-action correlations that support coordinated multi-agent futures. On D3IL, a benchmark of diverse human demonstrations, our trained models generate multiple obstacle-crossing routes from a common starting point without observed motion. On the controlled tasks, our classical and quantum prior implementations improve prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the evaluated variational baselines. Our quantum priors combine competitive predictive quality with a parameter-efficient sampling structure: they avoid an exponentially sized categorical output layer while supporting correlated latent actions. We further validate finite-shot parameter-shift training, including training with readout noise. Unlike most prior work, which focuses on simulation, we also verify the feasibility of inference with trained priors on a real QPU. These results establish a trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.
items.title: Quantum-JEPA: Quantum Born Priors for Latent-Action JEPA World Models

items.summary: Statistical learning in high dimensions suffers from the curse of dimensionality. Fortunately, many functions of practical interest are compositionally sparse, meaning they admit a composition of local functions, each depending on only a few variables, allowing sample complexity to depend on local arity rather than ambient dimension. Yet realizing this benefit requires exploiting hidden compositional structure, which theory does not establish for practical gradient-based training. We study this gap with CSFRBench, a controlled benchmark that hides the target's compositional computation during training but retains it for diagnosis, and find that dense networks and sparsity-based baselines leave much of that benefit unrealized. Inspired by the spatial organization of biological neural circuits, we introduce Learned Wiring (LeWi): each neuron has a learned low-dimensional embedding, only nearby neurons connect, and embeddings and weights are trained jointly. LeWi improves sample efficiency on targets with hierarchical structure, intermediate reuse, or independent modules. Across 32 additional targets generated by independently sampled computation graphs, LeWi is the most sample-efficient method not given the target graph, with 27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks. Dense networks perform better on targets with a single high-arity function. LeWi's representations and connectivity align with the target computation. On 17 world-model prediction tasks spanning control, navigation, and manipulation, LeWi beats the dense baseline on 16 and wins 99/119 baseline comparisons. These results show that jointly learning connectivity and weights can exploit computational structure to improve sample efficiency.
items.title: Learning Computational Structure for Sample-Efficient Prediction

items.summary: RTL repair benchmarks should measure whether a model can fix broken RTL given a specification. To this end, we construct and hash-bind RTLRepairDataset, 5,784 (broken, fixed) training pairs; RTLRepairBench, 459 held-out cases with 374 syntactic and 85 behavioral mutations; and an evaluation harness supporting simulation and formal equivalence. We then use this infrastructure to identify two measurement confounds. First, simulation and formal scoring give opposite signs for the apparent effect of providing a specification in one evaluated cohort; reset-aware rescoring attributes almost all of the simulation-formal disagreement to reset and first-cycle comparison semantics. Second, on 274 mined model failures, the specification-only minus specification-conditioned recovery point estimate ranges from -8.5 to +18.3 percentage points across six models. Thus, a conventional repair score need not isolate whether the model used the faulty RTL. We translate these findings into evaluation controls: report initialization, reset, first-cycle, and unknown-value semantics; disclose oracle coverage and undecided cases; and include a specification-only baseline. Together, the resources and audit provide both a benchmark for behavioral repair and a protocol for diagnosing what contributes to its measured score. We release the benchmark, the training set, construction code, sanitized aggregate evidence, and reproduction materials at https://github.com/Evaaaz/RTLRepairBench.
items.title: What Do RTL Repair Benchmarks Actually Measure?

items.summary: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
items.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines

items.summary: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.
items.title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models

items.summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4$\times$ fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1$\times$ faster with 9.6$\times$ less peak memory at low budgets.
items.title: RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting

items.summary: Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality is both a conditioning signal and a supervision target. We ask: can jointly generating language enrich this shared representation, improving manipulation and supporting memory-dependent behavior? Unlike prior approaches that attach a reasoning or vision-language model to a video-action backbone and run them as distinct stages, UniWALM unifies all three modalities inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone whose per-modality diffusion heads co-denoise synchronously, decoding subtask and textual memory in the same pass as action with no separate planning stage; the generated language is re-consumed on the next step, closing a language-as-memory loop without an external planner or memory bank. To keep the action stream reliable under this richer objective, we further introduce Flow Matching with Correction (FMC), a training objective that teaches recovery from perturbed action trajectories at no inference-time cost. UniWALM consistently improves over same-backbone baselines (e.g., FastWAM) on compositional pick-and-place (MolmoSpaces) and across the memory-dependent subset of RMBench, where it reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model and exceeds Mem-0's keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame. On a real-world Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% to 61.1%, while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance (<=33.3%).
items.title: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control

items.summary: Game engines and coding agents can specify the layout, motion, and camera of a scene, yet turning such coarse structure into realistic video requires a renderer that follows the structure and completes the appearance it leaves open. Existing renderers are tied to the representation of one engine, need tens of denoising steps or a costly distillation of their own, and learn from conditions that are not aligned with their target videos. We present SolarRenderer, a structure-conditioned video renderer that adapts a frozen MiniMax-H3 33B backbone with two lightweight LoRAs. Structural videos enter the native reference pathway of the backbone at the positions of the frames they describe, without a type identifier and described only in plain text, so that a single control LoRA follows arbitrary structural representations. Starting from a pretrained four-step LoRA, structure-guided distribution matching renders in four steps, 12.3 times faster than 50-step sampling, while preserving the learned control. A block-causal variant extends the same design to streaming and renders 768p video in real time. To train the model, we build a frame-aligned corpus of 136K clips from game engines, simulators, and YouTube videos. Experiments on an in-distribution test set and a generalization benchmark of 16 structural representations show that SolarRenderer achieves state-of-the-art results across both, and generalizes to 11 unseen representations, including pose skeletons, drawings, and point clouds.

items.summary: Patient Specific Regenerative Microfactories and Swarm Manufacturing at the Limit English Publication Description STARLI Flagship 22   30 Physicalized Models   82 Chapters   200 Research Gates Patient Specific Regenerative Microfactories and Swarm Manufacturing at the Limit is a high-density research monograph on manufacturing individualized cells, scaffolds, microtissues, and therapeutic components through distributed robotic systems without weakening lot release quality. The book treats every patient as a distinct manufacturing lot. Starting material, cell genealogy, material flow, agent action, calibration, environmental state, contamination evidence, identity, purity, maturation, and blind terminal function remain linked throughout production. Personalization changes the process path but never waives the release contract. Thirty physicalized models connect stochastic lot release, population dynamics, clonal diversity, living-product mass balance, contamination transport, Bayesian sterility, microfluidic residence time, oxygen and thermal transport, scaffold maturation, viscoelasticity, adhesion injury, swarm allocation, fault-bounded consensus, common-cause reliability, calibration drift, sensor fusion, change detection, small-lot inference, potency, multivariate release, logistics, recipe portability, provenance, economics, and robust joint qualification. Eighty-two chapters each open with a governing gold equation and develop five one-page research sections. Two hundred Research Gates challenge the system with donor shift, contamination, agent failure, supply interruption, calibration drift, reagent substitution, incomplete genealogy, and blinded transfer to a second laboratory. The work is a preclinical manufacturing research framework rather than a clinical protocol or release authorization. Contamination, identity failure, unclosed genealogy, invalid calibration, and failed independent function are noncompensable vetoes. Its Phoenix Answer Embryo, the Regenerative Microfactory Capsule, binds patient material, lineage, agent capability, process state, substitutions, deviations, blind potency, release, quarantine, and terminal disposition into one auditable and portable evidence object. items.summary: Description: Arduino firmware for the control unit of a low-cost, marble-type gas–water equilibrator used for continuous measurement of dissolved pCO₂ in inland waters. The firmware controls the water and gas pumps, reads a SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor and a DS18B20 water-temperature probe, and logs the data to an SD card with timestamps from a real-time clock. It accompanies the manuscript “A microcontroller-based, low-cost platform for continuous pCO₂ measurements in lakes and reservoirs” (Grochocki and Mannich, Limnology and Oceanography: Methods, under review). Hardware ·          Arduino Uno (ATmega328P) ·          SenseAir K30 NDIR CO₂ sensor, 0–10,000 ppm (UART/Modbus via SoftwareSerial; RX pin 3, TX pin 2) ·          DS18B20 waterproof temperature probe (OneWire, pin 6) ·          DS1307 real-time clock (I²C) ·          SD card module (SPI, CS pin 10) ·          Two-channel relay module: water pump (pin 7) and gas pump (pin 5) Operating cycle 1.       Switch on the water and gas pumps. 2.       For the duration of a measurement cycle, read CO₂ and water temperature at a fixed interval and append each reading to a daily file on the SD card. 3.       Switch off both pumps and stay idle until the next cycle. Configuration Timing parameters are read at boot from a config.txt file on the SD card, one key=value per line: ·          measurementInterval : idle time between cycles (minutes) ·          dataCollectionInterval : time between readings (seconds) ·          fullMeasurementTime : duration of each cycle (minutes) If the file does not exist, the firmware creates one with default values, which take effect at the next boot. The values hard-coded in the sketch are a 10-min cycle, 5-s readings and a 45-min idle period. Output One comma-separated text file per day, named YY-MM-DD.txt , with the header Date Time, CO2 (ppm), Water Temp (C) . Timestamps are written as YYYY-M-D H:M:S , without zero padding. Each file is opened and closed at every write, so data are not lost if power is cut. Notes ·          The CO₂ values logged are the raw K30 output. Calibration against a reference analyzer, conversion to pCO₂ (water-vapor and pressure correction) and conversion to dissolved CO₂ are done in post-processing, as described in the accompanying paper (Eqs. 1–5). ·          If the RTC has not been set, it is set at first boot to the compile time of the sketch. ·          The K30 automatic baseline correction (ABC) assumes regular exposure to ~400 ppm air, so it should be disabled for underwater use. Required libraries: SD, SPI, Wire, SoftwareSerial (Arduino core); OneWire; DallasTemperature; TimeLib; DS1307RTC.
